summary.heading: Reference frames and Galilean relativity
summary.html:
• A reference frame is a coordinate system with rulers and synchronised clocks that gives each event (something at one place and one instant) a position $x$ and time $t$.
  • An inertial frame is not accelerating; Newton's first law holds in it. Special relativity deals only with inertial frames.
  • Frame S′ moves at constant velocity $v$ along $x$ relative to S; clocks start at $t = t' = 0$ when the origins pass.
  • Galileo and Newton assumed time is absolute and lengths are the same for everyone:
$$x' = x - vt \qquad t' = t \qquad u' = u - v$$
  • Galilean relativity: both frames measure the same acceleration, so Newton's laws are the same in all inertial frames. No mechanics experiment inside a smoothly moving, closed train reveals its speed.

summary.heading: The problem with light and Einstein's postulates
summary.html:
• Maxwell's theory fixes the speed of light, $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}}$, without saying relative to what. Galilean addition would give different speeds for different observers.
  • The Michelson–Morley experiment (1887) looked for the Earth's motion through the "ether" and found no change in the speed of light.
1. The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames.
2. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers, whatever the motion of the source or observer.
  • So distances and times must differ between frames. There is no ether and no absolute frame.

summary.heading: Lorentz transformations and velocity addition
summary.html:
$$x' = \gamma(x - vt) \qquad t' = \gamma\left(t - \frac{vx}{c^2}\right)$$ $$\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}}}$$
  • Derivation not required. For intervals, use $\Delta x$ and $\Delta t$. To go back from S′ to S, swap the primes and change the sign of $v$.
  • $\gamma \ge 1$, and $\gamma \to \infty$ as $v \to c$. Useful values: $0.60c \to 1.25$, $0.80c \to 1.67$, $0.866c \to 2.0$.
  • At everyday speeds $\gamma \approx 1$, so the Galilean equations are an excellent approximation.
$$u' = \frac{u - v}{1 - \dfrac{uv}{c^2}}$$
  • Use signs (+ in the $+x$ direction). Two craft each moving at $0.60c$ towards each other (Earth frame): each measures the other approaching at $0.88c$, not $1.20c$. If $u = c$, then $u' = c$: no result exceeds $c$.

summary.heading: The space-time interval
summary.html:
$$(\Delta s)^2 = (c\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2$$
  • $(\Delta s)^2$ is invariant: the same in every inertial frame, even though $\Delta t$ and $\Delta x$ differ.
  • $(\Delta s)^2 > 0$: a signal slower than light can link the events, so one could cause the other and everyone agrees on their order.
  • $(\Delta s)^2 = 0$: the events can be linked only by light.
  • $(\Delta s)^2 < 0$: nothing can travel between them, and observers can disagree about which came first.

summary.heading: Time dilation and length contraction
summary.html:
$$\Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta t_0 \qquad L = \frac{L_0}{\gamma}$$
  • Proper time $\Delta t_0$: measured in the frame where both events happen at the same place (by a clock present at both). It is the shortest time; a moving clock runs slow.
  • Proper length $L_0$: measured in the object's rest frame. It is the longest length; moving objects are shorter, along the motion only.
  • The two effects go together: Earth says the astronaut's clock runs slow; the astronaut says the distance is contracted. Both agree on what the astronaut's clock reads on arrival.
  • Twin paradox: the travelling twin returns younger. The situation isn't symmetrical, because only the traveller changes inertial frame.
  • Derivations not required (the light clock is an optional illustration).

summary.heading: Simultaneity and space-time diagrams
summary.html:
• Relativity of simultaneity: events at the same time but different places in one frame are not simultaneous in a frame moving relative to it (from the $\dfrac{vx}{c^2}$ term). Events at the same place and time are simultaneous for everyone.
  • Space-time diagram: $x$ horizontal, $ct$ vertical. A body's path is its world line: vertical at rest, straight and tilted at constant velocity, 45° for light.
$$\tan\theta = \frac{v}{c}$$
  • $\theta$ is the angle between the world line and the $ct$ axis.
  • For S′: the $ct'$ axis is tilted by $\theta$ from $ct$; the $x'$ axis is tilted up by the same $\theta$ from $x$. Both tilt towards the 45° light line.
  • Read S′ coordinates with lines parallel to the $x'$ and $ct'$ axes. Events on a line parallel to the $x'$ axis are simultaneous in S′.
  • The scales on the tilted axes differ from those on $x$ and $ct$; they are fixed by lines of constant interval (hyperbolas). Time dilation, length contraction and simultaneity can all be shown on the diagram.

summary.heading: Evidence: muon decay
summary.html:
• Muons are made about 10 km up by cosmic rays and travel at about $0.995c$ ($\gamma \approx 10$). Mean lifetime at rest: about 2.2 µs.
  • Without relativity they would travel only about 660 m on average, so very few should reach the ground. Many do.
  • Earth's frame: time dilation stretches the lifetime to about 22 µs (about 6.6 km of travel).
  • Muon's frame: the lifetime is 2.2 µs, but the atmosphere is length-contracted to about 1 km.
  • Both views predict the same count, confirmed by measurements at different altitudes: evidence for time dilation and length contraction.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Getting proper time the wrong way round (it is the shortest, measured where both events are at the same place).
  • Getting proper length the wrong way round (it is the longest, measured at rest).
  • Adding velocities the Galilean way at high speed, giving answers above $c$.
  • Forgetting the signs in the velocity addition formula for objects moving towards each other.
  • Mixing units in $\dfrac{vx}{c^2}$ (watch out for µs).
  • Thinking only one observer is "right": they agree on $c$ and on the interval.
  • Drawing the $x'$ axis tilted downwards.

Theories: Show that $\gamma \approx 1$ for a jet airliner. Did special relativity overthrow Newton, or show where Newton works?
Why might scientists prefer a new theory that contains the old one as a special case?
Falsification: Michelson and Morley found nothing. Why was a null result so important, and why might it be hard to publish a null result today?
Some physicists tried to save the ether (for example with length contraction of the apparatus). When does rescuing an idea stop being reasonable?
Models: Einstein started from two postulates and deduced the rest. How is that different from building a model from measurements, as in A.1?
Does drawing relativity as geometry (space-time diagrams) give us new knowledge, or just a new picture of the same knowledge?
Evidence: GPS satellites must correct for relativity every day. Is technology that works stronger evidence than a laboratory experiment?
The muon result can be explained in either frame. Does having two explanations make the evidence stronger or weaker?

oracy.html:
Think–pair–share (1 minute alone, 3 minutes in pairs, then pairs report to the class). Claim: "Two spaceships pass at high speed, and each crew measures the other's clocks running slow. They can't both be right, so one ship must really be the moving one."

  • We think … because …
  • The postulate that matters here is …
  • The strongest objection to our view is …

Listen for: both are right; no inertial frame is preferred, and comparing distant clocks depends on simultaneity, which is relative.

Can reasoning alone tell us about the wo: Einstein predicted time dilation before it was measured. Would students have believed it without the muon and clock experiments?
Compare with mathematics: what is the difference between a proof and a physical prediction?
Is common sense a reliable guide?: List "obvious" ideas from earlier topics that turned out wrong (heavier things fall faster, motion needs a force, time is absolute). What do they have in common?
If common sense comes from slow, everyday experience, should we expect it to work at $0.99c$ or inside atoms?
What does it mean to say something \"rea: Use the lightning-and-train example: is there a single correct answer about which strike came first? What would "correct" even mean?
Why does it matter that observers always agree on the order of events that could be cause and effect?
Why did it take a paradigm shift?: Lorentz had the equations; Einstein changed what they meant. Is an interpretation part of scientific knowledge, or just a way of talking about it?
What might have made it hard for experienced physicists in 1905 to give up absolute time?
